books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

primary_sources: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835)

stimulus.text: “Amongst the novel objects that attracted my attention during my stay in the United States, nothing struck me more forcibly than the general equality of conditions. I readily discovered the prodigious influence which this primary fact exercises on the whole course of society, by giving a certain direction to public opinion, and a certain tenor to the laws. . . . The more I advanced in the study of American society, the more I perceived that the equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to be derived, and the central point at which all my observations constantly terminated.” — Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, Volume 1 (1835).
stimulus.source_note: Alexis de Tocqueville, Democracy in America, vol. 1 (1835), Introduction. Verbatim quotation (Reeve translation), verified against the Bill of Rights Institute excerpts. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Which development of the 1820s best explains why Tocqueville found the “equality of conditions” so striking?

options.misconception: The tariff divided regions over trade; it did not make ranks more equal.

options.text: Most states dropped property qualifications, opening voting to most free white men

options.misconception: That compromise drew a line for slavery's expansion; it did not change who could vote.

options.text: The completion of the Erie Canal in 1825 linking east and west
options.misconception: The canal moved goods and enriched New York; it did not flatten social rank.

rationales.A: The tariff fought over trade, not over who could vote.
rationales.B: As property rules fell in the 1820s, ordinary white men voted, held office, and joined parties, which made equality visible in daily politics.
rationales.C: The Missouri Compromise settled where slavery could spread, not who could vote.
rationales.D: The canal changed trade and transport, not social rank.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Tocqueville could see. He watched ordinary men vote, campaign, and join associations.
2. Find the cause. In the 1820s most states reduced or removed property qualifications for voting.
3. Rule out the rest. Tariffs, the Missouri line, and canals changed trade and territory, not who counted as a citizen.
Background: By 1840 about 90 percent of adult white men could vote, a share that startled European visitors.
Remember: a visitor notices what a country does in public, so start with the ballot box.
